stories.title: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
stories.summary: In her first earnings report as interim CEO, Nvidia's Colette Kress calmed investors' nerves, at least for the moment.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
sources.text: Five days after Nvidia 's Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded 33 years ago under a cloud of scandal, a nervous base of shareholders eagerly awaited Colette Kress' first public appearance as interim CEO. Following Nvidia's better-than-expected earnings report on Tuesday, Kress offered some relief to Wall Street, at least temporarily, by proclaiming on the call with analysts that customers are still fully onboard and that there's no slippage in demand. She said leadership from Nvidia's most important supplier, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company , visited company offices this week. "We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners, they're all 100% behind us," Kress said on the call. "Customers have expressed their support to the business outlook and helping us through that." While Huang was a singular figure in artificial intelligence with a commanding presence across the globe, Nvidia is still at the center of the AI ecosystem. Customers ranging from hyperscalers and neoclouds to frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic remain in persistent need of its technology and capital. Nvidia shares climbed almost 5% in extended trading on Tuesday after the chipmaker's better-than-expected earnings and strong guidance. That still leaves the stock in a deep slump after a 24% drop so far this month, driven by broad concerns about a slowdown in the AI buildout, a political handoff in Washington, D.C., and the turmoil at the top of the company. Despite all those headwinds and what Nvidia called the "unexpected transition" in leadership, the business is still booming. Revenue more than doubled in the latest quarter to $115.84 billion, and Nvidia projects roughly 90% growth in the current period to about $130 billion. More importantly, Kress said the 70% growth forecast for next year that was offered over the summer is actually too low. Now the projection is 75%. That's for a company that's seen revenue multiply by about 15-fold since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. While Huang is gone, "demand did not leave with him," Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives said in a note after the report. Kress maintained her optimistic tone in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer after the call. "The most important thing that we have been seeing is continuing growth in terms of the demand that's out there," she said. Kress also said on the call that Nvidia's stepped-up buybacks, announced in September, are still on track, confirming that the board had added $150 billion to the company's authorization for share repurchases. It's not all on Kress. The consistent message throughout the earnings call was that Nvidia is preparing for life after Huang. Harvey Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia's board, opened by saying that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," the first time the board had given a reason for his removal. A day earlier, CNBC reported that Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO. Kress said on the call that it's "business as usual." In a statement, she said the company's roadmap is "on track," indicating that there haven't been any changes to future chips and systems currently in development. Nvidia said that the Vera Rubin AI system is off to an "extraordinary start," selling $20 billion in the latest quarter. But Kress did signal a slight change to the company's willingness to backstop certain projects, and said Nvidia is being "disciplined" with how it's thinking about financing startups. "There's a lot of discussion internally with a lot of the teams on what we think are the best ones that we want to do," Kress told Cramer. "We're going to continue down that path to make sure we choose the right investments for us to work through going forward," Nvidia said its quarterly filing would be published in the "coming weeks," whereas it normally lands on the same day as earnings. On the call, neither Kress nor Jones addressed an avalanche of investigations and hearings in Washington looking into allegations that Nvidia was boosting revenue by selling chips to companies that are passthroughs for buyers in China. China only came up twice during the call. Kress said Nvidia had sold about $2.4 billion worth of approved data center products to China during the quarter, and that Nvidia had stopped selling licensed Hopper chips to China. Kress also noted that new trade rules released by the U.S. Commerce Department will cut off Chinese access to renting Nvidia chips. "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us and employees are committed," Kress said when signing off the call. "We've got this." WATCH: Nvidia out with 'very solid report'

sources.title: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
sources.text: Nvidia's customers and employees remain committed to the company despite last week's abrupt departure of longtime leader Jensen Huang . That's the message interim CEO Colette Kress conveyed exclusively to CNBC's Jim Cramer shortly after the AI chip giant delivered a quarterly beat and strong guidance. "[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," Kress said on " Mad Money ." "This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers." Kress' comments came after Nvidia reported better-than-expected quarterly earnings and revenue and bumped up its fiscal 2028 revenue growth estimate to 75% from the previous 70%. It was the first earnings report since Huang's resignation as CEO amid a widening affair scandal. Shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading as the results helped ease concerns about the chipmaker's outlook following the leadership shake-up. Some on Wall Street have wondered whether Huang's departure would prompt certain Nvidia customers to lean harder into their in-house designed chips and/or competitors such as Advanced Micro Devices . During the "Mad Money" interview Tuesday evening, Kress emphasized that major customers have continued expressing interest in the company's products. "I have seen already with many of these [customers] contacting me and saying, 'Great to see everything intact. Great to see that there's more supply. I need more demand.'" Customer demand, however, wasn't the only issue facing Nvidia. Huang's departure has also raised questions about whether the chipmaker can retain the engineers and other employees who helped build its dominance in artificial intelligence. The co-founder was widely viewed as the driving force behind Nvidia's technology and corporate culture. Kress dismissed concerns about a potential employee exodus, stressing to Cramer that the workforce's longstanding commitment to the company is intact, and so is support from the leadership team. "The company has been built under the perspective that the employees look at Nvidia as their life work, and many of them have been here for many decades, working with us both from a technology standpoint or a business and operations perspective," she said. "We have high confidence that our employees are definitely still working, still working with us, and enjoy ... the work here at Nvidia," Kress told Cramer. sources.title: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
sources.text: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress told employees "let's move forward" on Wednesday during the company's first all-hands meeting since founder Jensen Huang resigned, a person who attended the meeting told CNBC. The person asked not to be named because the meeting was private. Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones and hyperscale and high-performance computing head Ian Buck. Several other senior members of Nvidia's executive team spoke or joined Kress on stage, including longtime company veteran Jeff Fisher, senior vice president of software engineering Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of GPU engineering Jonah Alben, executive vice president in charge of operations Debora Shoquist and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, according to people familiar with the matter. Kress opened with the message about moving forward and also mentioned pay raises and explained that the yearly review process, when employees typically get pay raises and are granted more stock, would be moved up from March to December. Nvidia shares are down 37% from their 52-week high. Jones discussed the search for the next CEO, the person who attended the meeting said. The meeting lasted about an hour and was in person as well as streamed on Microsoft Teams. The general sentiment swirling in the room, according to the person, was that employees want Huang to come back . Employees have spoken up on X in recent days to call for the return of Huang as CEO, and one senior employee reportedly sent a letter to the board warning Nvidia would lose "irreplaceable talent" if it doesn't consider reinstating Huang. But another person familiar with the matter disagreed, saying that employees welcomed the remarks from leadership as well as the visibility into company leadership. The person asked not to be named because the matter is private. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday. Some executives shared that they do not agree with Jones. "Why make such a strong definitive statement when the investigation is still playing out," an employee told CNBC. The employee asked not to be named given the sensitivity of the subject. The meeting was held one day after Huang said he was ready to return as CEO should the board want him. Multiple employees told CNBC that Huang's letter "fired employees up." Despite recent turmoil, Wednesday's meeting was not out of the ordinary. Nvidia typically holds all-hands the morning after quarterly earnings reports, according to a former employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private. Kress recapped Tuesday's earnings report, calling it a "great quarter," according to the person who said employees welcomed the remarks and visibility from leadership. In past meetings, Huang took time to answer questions submitted by employees, according to the former employee. A person familiar with the matter told CNBC that the executives also answered pre-submitted questions in Wednesday's all-hands. Nvidia shares were down Wednesday, a day after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations and gave no signal that the company was going to slow its growth. Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that executives at Nvidia's all-hands meeting answered employee questions. A previous version mischaracterized how executives handled employee questions. WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huang

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
sources.text: As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO . And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back . At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.” Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” One recurring theme emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI. Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago. The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago. Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee. Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia AI technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions. On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation. Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia,” adding that he is “committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.” However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week. But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad , and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.” Huang’s activities are under investigation by at least four entities: the FBI and the US Department of Justice, Congress, the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and an independent law firm appointed by Nvidia’s board. Industry sources previously told WIRED that Huang is unlikely to return to the company anytime soon. Interim CEO Kress, at the end of Tuesday’s call, offered what sounded like a rallying cry for anyone doubting Nvidia’s future without Huang. “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed,” Kress said. “We’ve got this.”

sources.title: Inside Nvidia’s First Post-Jensen All-Hands: Pay Raises and More Equity
sources.text: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress made her first address to the staff on Wednesday and just minutes into the meeting told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of schedule, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp,” she said. Questions about compensation were the most common among the 700 submitted ahead of the meeting, Kress said. She said the next-most common request was for transparency from the board. Kress’ comments came during the first companywide meeting following the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO last week. Huang had led the computer graphics chip maker since cofounding it 33 years ago, and his presentations during the quarterly town halls internally had become a much anticipated and memorable spectacle for some of the company’s nearly 49,000 employees. Information rarely leaked from the meetings in the past. Nvidia declined to comment for this story. But now Nvidia is facing an extraordinary leadership crisis . Huang resigned amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including potentially with a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board chair Harvey Jones said on Tuesday that Huang disclosed “personal behavior” contrary to the company’s policies and norms and wouldn’t be invited back. During the companywide meeting on Wednesday, Jones reiterated that the board accepted Huang’s resignation due to his personal conduct and “lack of candor.” He said the company wouldn’t find a “Jensen clone,” but that there are “dynamic leaders out there, with demonstrated intellect, high-tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility, and a track record of success.” He added, “We will not compromise our requirements for the sake of expediency” and that the board would accept employee suggestions on the CEO search. Thousands of employees have apparently lobbied for Huang’s reinstatement. Several well-known tech executives signed a public petition, with about 200,000 purported backers urging the same. Instead, the board is searching internally and externally for a replacement at one of the world’s most valuable companies and one of the biggest drivers of the generative AI boom. Huang’s departures and a slew of government investigations into him and Nvidia have rattled investors. But on Tuesday, Nvidia reported better-than-expected financial results and forecast growing sales in the years to come. Shares were up about 5 percent on Wednesday. One concern investors have expressed is whether Nvidia might see a brain drain of top talent. Many employees have stayed at Nvidia for Huang and his vision. Nvidia could also be perceived as a less desirable place for new and emerging talent to work, with its leadership in flux, during an especially critical time as competition in the AI chips market grows. On Tuesday’s third-quarter earnings call, an analyst from Bank of America Securities asked Kress directly about her “message” to Nvidia investors about talent retention, as well as the company’s overall durability and financial strategy through this major upheaval. Kress replied that “probably the most important thing” company leaders are thinking through right now is stabilizing its employee ranks. “We are always thinking about our employees. Like every community out there, there are diverse opinions,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure they are safe and make sure the work can be done in the current environment.” In a brief question-and-answer session with Kress during the all-hands meeting Wednesday, Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky addressed how the company could maintain its prized culture going forward. He recalled how he, Huang, and other cofounders thought it was “nonsense” to put cultural values up on posters. Instead, they want it instilled in “the way you behave, the way you work together, and the way you work,” and he believes that will stand the test of time. “We’re going to be fine,” he said. Kress ended the meeting, which lasted about 50 minutes, by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game. In the third quarter, “every single person sings,” she said. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you, that you will help sing it. Nvidia, we’ve got this.” Updated: 11/18/2026 1:26 p.m. EST: Updated with new details on comments made during the Nvidia all-hands meeting.

sources.title: Does Nvidia Got This? Interim CEO Colette Kress Says It’s Got This
sources.text: Nvidia is going through it. The chipmaker’s iconic leader just resigned due to an international scandal, its stock has taken a hit, and it’s in a precarious position as it tries to maintain its dominance in the AI era. Following Jensen Huang’s ouster, the company’s interim CEO and still-CFO, Colette Kress, has been tasked with stabilizing the deck. So far, Kress’ public-facing duties have included running the company’s third-quarter earnings call and hosting an all-hands meeting for Nvidia’s money-hungry workforce . And as part of her calming campaign, Kress has also been deploying a catchphrase that sounds like it was taken straight from the draft files of a summer of ’24 Democratic campaign strategist: “We’ve got this.” By WIRED’s count, Kress has publicly used the phrase three times in the past 24 hours, often putting emphasis or a little bit of zhuzh in it: “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this.” “Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change. We thank you all for the great quarter that we had. Just remember, we’ve got this.” Kress ended Wednesday’s meeting by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game, all singing together. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song … Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. But Nvidia, we’ve got this.” Kress’ new catchphrase perhaps isn’t the most inspiring; companies that got this usually don’t have to remind people how much they got this twice in one meeting. It’s a collectivist’s version of “You got this,” a slightly less corny version of “Yes we can,” a saying that may well pose more questions than it answers. (We got … what?) Nvidia investors, or any investor, might not have fist-pumped and said “We’ve got this!” during a quick portfolio check these past 10 days. Anyone who has had the slightest hint of knowledge that Nvidia’s chips were finding their way into China is unlikely to be in a “We totally got this” mood at the moment. Still, some Nvidia employees appear to be inspired by Kress’ mantra. “Damn right we got this,” Aaron Erickson, Nvidia’s head of NemoClaw engineering, posted on X on Wednesday. Vega Shah, who works in portfolio management for Nvidia’s venture capital arm, shared Erickson’s post and echoed the phrase , adding her own rocket ship emoji to the post. And yesterday, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang, despite some calls on social media and within the company to put Huang back in the top spot. Which means that Kress, for the moment, has … got this.

sources.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella remains confident in Nvidia after Huang’s exit
sources.text: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella weighed in on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unexpected departure amid a series of shocking controversies . “It’s all sort of pretty tragic in the sense of, you know, Jensen is somebody I’ve known for a long time. I’ve admired what he’s done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out,” Nadella said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. Huang stepped down last week from his CEO role, which he has held for 33 years. Huang’s leadership has been central to Nvidia’s ascent to one of the world’s most valuable companies, but his judgment was questioned after it was reported that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing. It was also revealed that Huang was having affairs with two Nvidia employees, including one who was a direct report. While the world waits to see what the long-term economic impacts of Huang’s departure might be, Nadella says he still has confidence in Nvidia, which is a close partner of Microsoft. “I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella added. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO at Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I’m in touch with the same set of people I was in touch with before [Huang left], so I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.” Microsoft is not unlike Nvidia in that its founder Bill Gates inhabited a larger-than-life persona as CEO. “Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing, so that is pretty magical… They’re singular, but they’re not gods, right?” Nadella said. “I used to say to Bill [Gates]… Founders also die, and so at some point, a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Amanda Silberling is a senior writer at TechCrunch covering the intersection of technology and culture. She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she worked as a grassroots organizer, museum educator, and film festival coordinator. She holds a B.A. in English from the University of Pennsylvania and served as a Princeton in Asia Fellow in Laos. stories.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
stories.summary: Turn Gemini’s annotations into an edge model for manufacturing inspection. Explore three prompting approaches, review labels, and train RF-DETR model with Roboflow. Deploy the trained model near the camera and keep Gemini available to inspect difficult cases and improve future training data.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: How to Distill Gemini Into an Edge Model
sources.text: To distill Gemini into an edge model, have Gemini label your images, review and correct those labels, then train a small detector that runs next to the camera and does the routine inspections. In Roboflow, auto-label with Gemini through a class description, the Auto Label agent or an Open Prompt Workflow. Then train RF-DETR Small on the reviewed dataset, run it with Inference on your edge device, and route uncertain cases back to Gemini or a human reviewer. Checking an assembly for missing screws takes more than counting detections. A model might miss one screw and mistake a reflection for another, returning the expected count while overlooking an incomplete product. A useful inspection system needs to locate the visible screws at each mounting position and flag images that need further review. With Roboflow, you can use Gemini to help build the training dataset for that system, then train a compact RF-DETR (opens in a new tab) model to detect screws near the camera. In this approach to model distillation , Gemini generates candidate bounding boxes, you review and correct the annotations, and RF-DETR learns the specific detection task. At deployment, the smaller model handles routine detection, while routing logic sends selected difficult images to Gemini or a person for review. In this guide, you’ll explore three ways to prompt Gemini for screw annotations: class descriptions in Roboflow Auto Label, conversational feedback with the Auto Label agent, and an Open Prompt Workflow that returns boxes for inspection in Python. You’ll then review the labels, train RF-DETR Small, test it on your edge hardware, and configure a fallback for uncertain results. Before generating labels, decide exactly what one object means. In our reference image, each screw annotation covers the full visible fastener region, including its outer exposed end and inner metal feature. One screw receives one box. This definition must stay the same across the dataset. Create an Object Detection project and upload the product images (opens in a new tab) . Include complete products, missing screws, reflections, and realistic changes in lighting. In Roboflow Auto Label , the class description is the prompt Gemini uses to find the object . Follow these steps. Gemini searches using that description, and Auto Label saves each resulting annotation as screw . The expected count of four is an application rule. It should not force the teacher to produce four boxes when a screw is missing. You can also describe the labeling task through Chat with Auto Label agent . The agent builds a labeling Workflow from the model and classes and shows a preview. Use the conversation to refine what it should label. The saved annotations still need a class name, which remains screw in this example. See labeling with the Auto Label agent (opens in a new tab) . With Gemini 4 Carbon selected, open Chat with Auto Label agent and enter the following request. Check the preview and request specific corrections. You can use the following correction when that error appears. You can also click an incorrect label or use Flag missing object. Once the preview matches the annotation rule, choose Use this Workflow, confirm the output-class mapping to screw , and select Label batch. Review the job estimate before starting. Continue with the label review in Section 2. This conversation configures the Auto Label Workflow. Gemini 4 Carbon remains the requested annotation model. Check that the saved Workflow uses it. Either setup option produces the same kind of training data for RF-DETR Small. The training examples contain reviewed screw bounding boxes. For this option, you can choose any Gemini model available in the Roboflow Google Gemini block (opens in a new tab) that supports image input and Open Prompt. You can also try different available models with the same prompt and images to compare their bounding boxes. For the Auto Label process above, Roboflow manages the saved annotations. Use the description field or the Auto Label agent conversation above. Neither option requires you to enter a JSON-format prompt or convert coordinates yourself. If you inspect raw Gemini detection output, Google's official object detection documentation (opens in a new tab) specifies box_2d in [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] order, normalized to 0–1000. Normalization expresses a position relative to the image dimensions. A value of 500 is halfway across the relevant dimension, regardless of image size. Use the following conversion for an image of width W and height H. For example, [100, 200, 300, 250] on a 1000-pixel-wide, 600-pixel-high image gives pixel bounds xmin=200, ymin=60, xmax=250, ymax=180. This is a coordinate example, not a measured screw prediction. Prompting Gemini for boxes in a consistent format gives the visualization code a clear schema to check. Gemini models can still format their answers differently even when they receive the same instructions. This Open Prompt test uses a consistent box_2d schema and a model-independent parser. The prompt requests the screw label and [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] coordinates normalized to 0–1000. The script accepts known JSON formatting differences, but checks the coordinates before drawing them. This follows Gemini’s object-detection coordinate convention (opens in a new tab) . The parser uses the requested coordinate order and scale. Numeric checks alone cannot prove that Gemini followed those instructions, so inspect the drawn boxes. Build this small test separately from Auto Label. Use an image input, a text input for the prompt, one Google Gemini block, and two outputs. Follow Build a Workflow (opens in a new tab) . Test with an assembly image and supply the example text in the Workflow’s prompt input. Confirm that both outputs, boxes_json and prompt_echo , appear in the test response. Save the Workflow and use Deploy (opens in a new tab) to copy its workspace slug, Workflow ID, and API URL for Python. Open Prompt returns raw text,

sources.title: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how
sources.text: You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI. Google likes to use your conversations with Gemini for model training to help improve the AI. But for people with privacy concerns, the only way to opt out of this was to delete your entire chat history. Now, Google is overhauling the process to eliminate that drawback. Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road. Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two. To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training. Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes “With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email. Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats. Almost all AIs include a setting for model training that you typically have to manually disable if you’re concerned about your privacy. But most let you opt out without turning off your chat history. ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.” Also: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027 (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.) In all those cases, you still retain access to your conversation history. In contrast, Google has been the only AI player among the majors to impose a restriction for those who want to opt out of AI training. Based on past actions, Google has often earned a reputation for being privacy-unfriendly. I’m glad to see the company take this step in the right direction. sources.title: Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents
sources.text: REDMOND, Wash. — Nov. 17, 2026 — Organizations can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they often cannot reconstruct what happened between a request and an outcome, making it difficult to independently verify model behavior. At Microsoft Ignite on Tuesday, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella announced the next phase of Microsoft’s commitment to making AI safer: the AI Transparency Initiative, a collaborative effort with customers and partners to establish a common, open approach to security and governance across models and providers. The initiative reflects a simple principle: Greater AI autonomy requires greater transparency. “For security controls to be effective, every organization needs greater transparency into the model itself,” said Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security. “With this work, we will bring more transparency to all models. This is a critical step in making containment smarter and stronger, allowing us to better inform accountability and traceability.” Enterprises are connecting AI models to data, tools, credentials and infrastructure, enabling agents to take actions without human approval at every step. Existing controls can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they cannot see what happens within them or independently verify their accounts of their own behavior. This limits organizations’ ability to understand the context behind an agent’s actions. That evidence gap creates security, compliance, audit and accountability risk. Security teams need a new trust architecture to address the growing insider risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents. “As AI agents become more deeply integrated into enterprise operations, security teams need clear visibility into what those agents are accessing, what actions they’re taking and how those actions can be verified,” said Aanchal Gupta, Chief Security Officer, Adobe. “Building a common approach to AI transparency across the industry is essential to strengthening trust and helping organizations innovate with confidence while maintaining security and accountability.” The initiative has three parts. First, Microsoft will expand its participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s SI Agent Standards Initiative and draw on its research to develop open, industrywide standards for AI transparency, security and governance. Second, Microsoft is collaborating with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to help develop open standards for AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Third, Microsoft will incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot, enabling customers to use the resulting evidence with their security and compliance tools, whether from Microsoft or other providers. “Our clients want to move faster with AI, and they shouldn’t have to choose between innovation and safety,” said John Israel, Global Chief Information Security Officer, KPMG International. “Trust in AI requires transparency, explainability and responsible oversight. We’re proud to work with Microsoft on the AI Transparency Initiative to help establish open, industrywide standards that give organizations the visibility and control they need to deploy AI responsibly at scale.” Agents with access to data, tools and credentials carry the risk profile of a privileged insider but operate at machine speed and scale, making independent oversight essential. Accountability stays with the organization. When something consequential happens, leaders answer to customers, employees, boards, auditors and regulators. Blaming the AI isn’t an answer, and “trust the model” isn’t a control. The initiative is designed to work across models and providers, including closed and open-weight models, so developer teams can change or update the models powering their agents without compromising IT and security teams’ ability to govern them securely or compliance teams’ ability to audit their actions. “As organizations take the next step in their AI reinventions, they need a solid foundation of trust and confidence to build from,” said Harpreet Sidhu, global cybersecurity lead, Accenture. “Initiatives like this from Microsoft to take an open, industry-driven approach to AI transparency can help as we secure AI models and fit them with controls and governance. Accenture is proud to partner with Microsoft and other leaders in this space.” Microsoft believes every organization should be able to see what AI systems access and do, verify their actions independently and control what they are permitted to do. Organizations interested in helping shape the initiative or following its progress can learn more and sign up at aka.ms/learnmoreAItransparency . Follow the news from Microsoft Ignite, where Microsoft and industry leaders will share insights on how organizations can manage AI models and agents with confidence. More is available on the Microsoft Security blog . Microsoft Media Relations, We. sources.title: Introducing Roboflow Organizations for Enterprise
sources.text: Roboflow Organizations for Enterprise lets you roll vision AI out across departments and business units, while each team keeps its own Workspace, members, data and spending controls. Leaders get one dashboard for adoption and deployment volume, plus SSO, custom roles, export-control restrictions and credit reallocation across Workspaces. Over 80,000 organizations build with Roboflow, including teams at over half of the Fortune 100. Enterprises like Rivian, BNSF Railway , and USG use Roboflow to make visual intelligence part of their operations. Roboflow customers often begin with a small, nimble team deploying successful vision solutions using Roboflow, and want to quickly expand their solutions and Roboflow tooling across the rest of the enterprise without worrying about complex data and billing concerns. The most successful enterprises scale AI impact by ensuring that problems aren’t solved in silos, while retaining control, visibility, and delineation across teams. Today, we’re introducing Organizations. An Organization (opens in a new tab) brings multiple Workspaces together under one umbrella. Organizations let large enterprises scale vision AI capabilities across departments, units, and projects. Each Workspace keeps its own members, projects, data, internal spending controls, and access controls. Keeping those workspaces separate ensures teams within the organization can move quickly and adopt new capabilities without sacrificing organizational control and visibility. Most of the enterprises we work with ask: The Organization Dashboard answers those questions with a view of member activity, projects, deployment volume, and adoption trends across Workspaces. Often, enterprises have business units or teams subject to compliance or standards, whether from customers, internal policy, or because they operate in a regulated industry. Roboflow’s Enterprise controls include single sign-on, custom roles, folder permissions, and restrictions on access to export-controlled data. This means that a business unit handling regulated or commercially sensitive data can operate in a dedicated Workspace, with limited and controlled access, while not placing undue restrictions on other business units without such regulatory requirements. Leaders also need to understand credit usage and control spending. A dedicated page within the Organization Dashboard allows insight into where credits go across different departments, teams or units (organized by Workspace) and even more granularly into individual project folders. It supplies business leaders with the context necessary to allocate costs to sites and projects, plan next year’s use cases, and reallocate unused credits across Workspaces as team needs change. As enterprises expand their use of Roboflow, we’re making it easier to bring new teams onto the platform and manage access and usage across Workspaces. We will also be expanding Roboflow Organizations to support vendors that offer Roboflow-powered products to their own customers. Many enterprises already use Roboflow to build their company-wide vision program with Roboflow. Organization dashboards are available today on select enterprise workspaces. Please reach out to our team to get started rolling out vision AI to your organization.
